playbooks.title: LifeOS Setup
playbooks.description: Installs Daniel Miessler's LifeOS — the AI-powered Life Operating System (formerly PAI, Personal AI Infrastructure) — onto a Claude Code or other agent. LifeOS v6 ships as one self-contained skill that installs additively (never clobbering your other files). The agent detects the harness and config root, drops the skill, then drives the install Tools to deploy Core (skill + ~50-skill library + LIFEOS runtime + system prompt + lifeos launch command) plus the chosen enhancements, wires hooks and the launch alias, and verifies with real evidence. The user runs /lifeos-setup afterwards for the Interview (TELOS current→ideal state) that seeds Pulse. Non-Claude harnesses get a degraded-but-real install; chat-only assistants fail the capability gate.
playbooks.author: Pedram Amini
playbooks.prompt:
# LifeOS Setup Agent Prompt

**IMPORTANT: Configure the placeholders below before running this playbook.**

LifeOS installs *additively* — it never clobbers your other files — but it is not *isolated* by default. In `user` scope the skill (and any hooks) land in the shared `~/.claude` and become visible to every Claude Code agent on this machine. Use `project` scope for genuine single-agent isolation.

## Configuration

### Components

<!-- CONFIGURE: Which à-la-carte enhancements to install. Comma-separated subset of hooks,statusline,tooltips,spinnerverbs,agents,pulse,worksweep,derivedsync — or `none`. Core (skill + skill library + LIFEOS runtime + system prompt + launch command) always installs regardless. `hooks` (Claude Code only) lights up the mode banner, memory loop, voice, and per-turn context injection. launchd components (pulse/worksweep/derivedsync) are macOS-only. -->
**LIFEOS_ENHANCEMENTS:** `hooks`

<!-- Examples:
- hooks,statusline,pulse   (recommended full Claude Code setup on macOS)
- hooks                    (default — always-on behavior, no dashboard)
- none                     (Core only)
-->

### Launch command

<!-- CONFIGURE: Whether to append the `lifeos` shell alias so the constitution (LIFEOS_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md) loads. Without it, Core is installed but a plain `claude` session runs un-constituted. yes / no. -->
**WIRE_LAUNCH_ALIAS:** `yes`

### Scope

<!-- CONFIGURE: Where LifeOS installs. `user` = shared ~/.claude (skill + hooks visible to every Claude Code agent on this machine). `project` = <AGENT_PATH>/.claude, scoped to this agent only (true single-agent isolation). Pulse's launchd service is machine-wide regardless. user / project. -->
**INSTALL_SCOPE:** `user`

## Agent Instructions

You are the AI LifeOS is being handed to. The user consented by launching this Auto Run, so self-consent at each mutation and drive the install Tools directly — do not wait for interactive approval. The install is additive: never clobber a populated file, never mutate the LifeOS source tree, and never write a harness config it won't read. Once the skill is dropped, its shipped `INSTALL.md` and `Workflows/Setup.md` are the authoritative, version-matched source for exact Tool flags and ordering — follow them. This playbook automates the logistics only; the Interview (identity + TELOS current→ideal state, which seeds Pulse) is a human conversation the user runs afterwards via `/lifeos-setup`.

launch.intro: Installs LifeOS into your coding harness, verifies it, and writes a setup summary with the exact next step.

requires: curl, bash and tar (bun is installed if missing)

inputs.name: LIFEOS_ENHANCEMENTS
inputs.label: Enhancements
inputs.help: Optional extras on top of Core. Pick none for Core only.

inputs.name: WIRE_LAUNCH_ALIAS
inputs.label: Add the lifeos shell alias
inputs.help: Without it, Claude Code does not load the LifeOS constitution.

outro.title: LifeOS setup finished
outro.summary: The verdict and the full summary are in `LIFEOS_SETUP.md` in the Auto Run folder.
nextSteps: Start a shell, run `lifeos`, then run `/lifeos-setup` to do the interview.
If you installed Pulse, open http://localhost:31337.
On FAILED or BLOCKED, read `LIFEOS_INSTALL_LOG.md`. The usual fix is installing bun.

playbooks.title: PR Bot Thread Cleanup
playbooks.description: Systematically cleans up unresolved CodeRabbit and Greptile PR review threads by separating stale bot comments from real findings, applying small validated fixes, and resolving newly stale threads after each push.
playbooks.author: Jeff Scott Ward
playbooks.prompt:
# PR Bot Thread Cleanup Agent Prompt

**IMPORTANT: Configure the placeholders below before running this playbook.**

---

## Configuration

### Target Pull Request

<!-- CONFIGURE: Full GitHub URL of the PR whose bot threads should be cleaned up. Required — the playbook will not infer this. -->
**PR_URL:** `https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/pull/XXX`

### Bot Reviewers in Scope

<!-- CONFIGURE: Comma-separated list of bot reviewer login names (or matching prefixes). Threads from reviewers outside this list are ignored. -->
**BOT_REVIEWERS:** `coderabbitai,greptile`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `coderabbitai,greptile`             — recommended default; the two most common review bots
- `coderabbitai`                      — CodeRabbit only
- `coderabbitai,greptile,sourcery-ai` — also include Sourcery
- `coderabbitai,greptile,bito-bot,qodo-merge` — broad sweep
-->

---

## Agent Instructions

This playbook cleans up unresolved PR review threads from automated review bots. Each loop iteration: re-fetches PR state, lists unresolved bot-authored threads, evaluates each as actionable vs. stale, applies a small validated batch of fixes, pushes, and re-polls. Loop exits when no `PENDING` bot findings remain.

The numbered task documents reference the configured variables as `[VARIABLE_NAME]` placeholders — substitute the configured values throughout. In particular:

- `[PR_URL]` is the target fetched in document 1 and re-polled each iteration
- `[BOT_REVIEWERS]` defines the in-scope reviewer login names for thread filtering in documents 2 and 4

Human review threads are always ignored regardless of `BOT_REVIEWERS` — this playbook does not touch threads authored by people.

launch.intro: Works through bot review threads on one pull request: fixes what is right, replies to what is wrong, and resolves each thread.

requires: Pushes commits to the pull request branch

inputs.name: BOT_REVIEWERS
inputs.label: Bot reviewers
inputs.help: Comma-separated GitHub logins. Threads from anyone else are left alone.

outro.title: Bot thread cleanup finished
outro.summary: The verdict (ACCEPT_READY or BLOCKED) is in `FINAL_SUMMARY.md`. Every thread and what happened to it is in `BOT_THREAD_LEDGER.md`.
nextSteps: Check any threads the ledger marks MANUAL or BLOCKED.
When the verdict is ACCEPT_READY, review the pushed commits and merge.

playbooks.title: Security Audit
playbooks.description: Comprehensive security analysis identifying vulnerabilities, outdated dependencies, and OWASP top 10 issues. Automatically remediates CRITICAL and HIGH severity issues.
playbooks.author: Pedram Amini
playbooks.prompt:
# Security Audit Agent Prompt

**IMPORTANT: Configure the placeholders below before running this playbook.**

---

## Configuration

### Auto-Fix Policy

The playbook auto-remediates only findings that match BOTH the severity AND remediability filters below. Findings outside these filters are routed to `PENDING - MANUAL REVIEW` (CRITICAL/HIGH but harder to fix) or `WON'T DO` (low impact).

<!-- CONFIGURE: Comma-separated severity levels eligible for auto-fix. Findings outside this list are not auto-remediated. -->
**AUTO_FIX_SEVERITY:** `CRITICAL,HIGH`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `CRITICAL,HIGH`        — recommended default; fix high-impact issues only
- `CRITICAL`             — most conservative; only the most urgent
- `CRITICAL,HIGH,MEDIUM` — aggressive; also auto-fix defense-in-depth issues
- Valid levels: CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, INFO
-->

<!-- CONFIGURE: Comma-separated remediability tiers eligible for auto-fix. Tiers outside this list are flagged for manual triage instead. -->
**AUTO_FIX_REMEDIABILITY:** `EASY,MEDIUM`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `EASY,MEDIUM`         — recommended default; skip fixes that need architectural changes
- `EASY`                — most conservative; only mechanical / one-line fixes
- `EASY,MEDIUM,HARD`    — aggressive; attempt complex refactors too
- Valid tiers: EASY, MEDIUM, HARD, VERY HARD
-->

---

## Agent Instructions

You are a security audit agent. Each loop runs the full pipeline against the target codebase: analyze attack surface → find specific vulnerabilities → rate severity and remediability → fix the in-scope ones → check whether more loops are needed. The loop exits when no findings match the configured `AUTO_FIX_SEVERITY` × `AUTO_FIX_REMEDIABILITY` policy.

The numbered task documents reference the variables above by name. Where you see `[AUTO_FIX_SEVERITY]` or `[AUTO_FIX_REMEDIABILITY]` in those docs, substitute the values you configured here — do not use the inline default literals.

launch.intro: Loops over your codebase: analyze, find candidates, evaluate them, apply the ones inside the tiers you pick, and log every change. Anything outside those tiers is left for you to review.

requires: The agent's working directory is a git repository of the project to change

outro.title: Security audit finished
outro.summary: Fixes inside the tiers you picked are applied and logged. Other findings are listed for manual triage.
nextSteps: Read the change log `SECURITY_LOG_{{AGENT_NAME}}_{{DATE}}.md` in the Auto Run folder.
Check the last `LOOP_N_PLAN.md` for candidates left for manual review.
Review the diff and run your test suite before committing.

playbooks.title: Code Refactoring
playbooks.description: Systematic code improvement targeting duplication, complexity, and large files. Implements safe, high-value refactors with LOW risk and HIGH benefit.
playbooks.author: Pedram Amini
playbooks.prompt:
# Code Refactoring Agent Prompt

**IMPORTANT: Configure the placeholders below before running this playbook.**

---

## Configuration

### Complexity Thresholds

Files/functions exceeding these thresholds are flagged as refactoring candidates. Tune per codebase — a Rails app and a Go service have different norms.

<!-- CONFIGURE: Files larger than this (in LOC) are flagged for splitting. -->
**MAX_FILE_LOC:** `500`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `500`   — recommended default for application code
- `300`   — strict; suitable for libraries
- `1000`  — relaxed; for codebases with many large auto-generated files
-->

<!-- CONFIGURE: Functions larger than this (in LOC) are flagged for breaking into smaller steps. -->
**MAX_FUNCTION_LOC:** `50`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `50`    — recommended default
- `30`    — strict; favors tight composition
- `100`   — relaxed; for service handlers with linear flows
-->

<!-- CONFIGURE: Functions nested deeper than this (if/else/switch levels) are flagged for extraction. -->
**MAX_NESTING_DEPTH:** `3`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `3`     — recommended default
- `2`     — strict; encourages guard clauses and early returns
- `4`     — relaxed; tolerates some embedded validation flows
-->

<!-- CONFIGURE: Functions with more parameters than this are flagged for extraction to a config object. -->
**MAX_PARAMETERS:** `5`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `5`     — recommended default
- `4`     — strict; pushes builder/options patterns
- `7`     — relaxed; for low-level adapters and constructors
-->

### Auto-Implement Policy

The playbook auto-applies refactors that match BOTH the risk AND benefit filters below. Refactors outside these filters are flagged for manual review or skipped.

<!-- CONFIGURE: Comma-separated risk tiers eligible for auto-refactor. Tiers outside this list are flagged for manual triage. -->
**AUTO_IMPLEMENT_RISK:** `LOW`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `LOW`         — recommended default; only mechanical refactors with full test coverage
- `LOW,MEDIUM`  — aggressive; accept some structural changes
- Valid tiers: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, VERY HIGH
-->

<!-- CONFIGURE: Comma-separated benefit levels eligible for auto-refactor. Levels outside this list are deprioritized. -->
**AUTO_IMPLEMENT_BENEFIT:** `HIGH,VERY HIGH`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `HIGH,VERY HIGH`  — recommended default; only meaningful improvements
- `VERY HIGH`       — most conservative; only architectural wins
- `MEDIUM,HIGH,VERY HIGH` — aggressive; cleanup nice-to-haves too
- Valid levels: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, VERY HIGH
-->

---

## Agent Instructions

You are a refactoring agent. Each loop runs the full pipeline against the target codebase: analyze structure → find specific candidates exceeding the complexity thresholds → rate each by risk and benefit → apply the in-scope refactors → check whether more work remains. The loop exits when no candidates match the configured `AUTO_IMPLEMENT_RISK` × `AUTO_IMPLEMENT_BENEFIT` policy.

The numbered task documents reference the variables above by name. Where you see `[MAX_FILE_LOC]`, `[MAX_FUNCTION_LOC]`, `[MAX_NESTING_DEPTH]`, `[MAX_PARAMETERS]`, `[AUTO_IMPLEMENT_RISK]`, or `[AUTO_IMPLEMENT_BENEFIT]` in those docs, substitute the values you configured here — do not use the inline default literals.

# Documentation Coverage Agent Prompt

**IMPORTANT: Configure the placeholders below before running this playbook.**

## Configuration

### Coverage Target

<!-- CONFIGURE: Documentation coverage threshold (% of in-scope exports that must have docs). The pipeline loops until coverage reaches this value or no eligible PENDING items remain. -->

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `90%`  — recommended default; high bar, suitable for libraries and public APIs
- `80%`  — pragmatic baseline for application code
- `100%` — strictest; every in-scope export must be documented
- `70%`  — minimum-viable for legacy codebases just starting to adopt docs
-->

The playbook auto-documents only exports that match BOTH the visibility AND importance filters below. Exports outside these filters are routed to `WON'T DO` (low visibility/importance) or `PENDING - NEEDS CONTEXT` (higher impact but require maintainer input).

<!-- CONFIGURE: Comma-separated visibility tiers eligible for auto-documentation. Exports outside this list are not auto-documented. -->
**AUTO_DOC_VISIBILITY:** `PUBLIC,INTERNAL`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `PUBLIC,INTERNAL`             — recommended default; document everything used across modules
- `PUBLIC`                      — most conservative; document only the public API surface
- `PUBLIC,INTERNAL,UTILITY`     — aggressive; also document helpers
- Valid tiers: PUBLIC, INTERNAL, UTILITY, IMPLEMENTATION
-->

<!-- CONFIGURE: Comma-separated importance levels eligible for auto-documentation. Levels outside this list are flagged for manual triage instead. -->
**AUTO_DOC_IMPORTANCE:** `CRITICAL,HIGH`

- `CRITICAL,HIGH`        — recommended default; document widely-used and non-obvious exports
- `CRITICAL`             — most conservative; only core, error-prone surface
- `CRITICAL,HIGH,MEDIUM` — aggressive; document moderately-used exports too
- Valid levels: CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW
-->

---

## Agent Instructions

Each loop runs the full pipeline against the target codebase: measure current coverage → find undocumented exports → rate each by visibility and importance → write docs for the in-scope ones → check whether the coverage target has been met. playbooks.title: Market Research
playbooks.description: Builds queryable Obsidian-style knowledge vaults about a market. Establishes a scope boundary before any research begins, scores every entity for membership as well as priority, stores facts in YAML frontmatter with typed relations, and validates corpus integrity on every loop.
playbooks.author: Pedram Amini
playbooks.prompt:
# Market Research Agent Prompt

**IMPORTANT: Configure the values below before running this playbook.**

Every value marked `<UNSET ...>` must be replaced. `0_CONFIGURE.md` refuses to
run while any required one is still at its default, so a half-configured run
costs you nothing instead of thirty loops of the wrong market.

---

## Research Configuration

### Target Market

<!-- CONFIGURE (required): what market to research. Be specific: a narrow
     market yields a far better vault than a broad one. -->
**MARKET_TOPIC:** `<UNSET - describe the market in three to six words>`

<!-- Examples:
- "Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure"
- "AI-Powered Developer Tools"
- "Plant-Based Meat Alternatives"
- "Enterprise Kubernetes Platforms"
- "Direct-to-Consumer Hearing Aids"
- "Carbon Capture Technologies"
-->

### Scope Boundary

The single most important thing you configure. Every market has a confusable
adjacent market that shares its vocabulary, and without a stated boundary a
long research run absorbs that neighbor one defensible entity at a time until
the vault is a generic industry list.

State the boundary as an **antonym pair**: what is in, and the specific
near-miss that is out. The out side should be a real, well-funded market that
sounds like yours - if it reads as obviously irrelevant, you have not found the
actual boundary yet.

<!-- CONFIGURE (optional but strongly recommended): if you leave these unset,
     0_CONFIGURE proposes a pair from a short market survey and writes it to
     SCOPE.md marked agent-proposed, for you to review. Setting them yourself
     is better. -->
**SCOPE_IN:** `<UNSET - one sentence: what belongs in this vault>`
**SCOPE_OUT:** `<UNSET - one sentence: the adjacent market that does not>`

<!-- Worked examples of the pattern:

  Market:    Carbon technology
  SCOPE_IN:  Carbon removal - technologies that are net-negative
  SCOPE_OUT: Carbon reduction - technologies that are merely less-positive

  Market:    Clinical software
  SCOPE_IN:  Systems that inform a diagnosis or treatment decision
  SCOPE_OUT: Systems that manage scheduling, billing and back-office workflow

  Market:    Robotics
  SCOPE_IN:  General-purpose manipulation in unstructured environments
  SCOPE_OUT: Fixed-function industrial automation on a known production line

  Market:    Payments
  SCOPE_IN:  Infrastructure for regulated money movement
  SCOPE_OUT: Consumer applications built on top of that infrastructure

Notice that in each pair the out side is legitimate and adjacent, not absurd.
The test is usually "which party is the beneficiary" or "which asset is the
one being served", never "which words appear on the homepage".
-->

### Domain Entity Type

Five entity types are generic to every market: Company, Product, Category,
Person, Capital. Most markets also have one object that people in that market
talk about constantly and that fits none of the five. Naming it is what turns a
copied template into a modeled market.

<!-- CONFIGURE (optional): leave unset and 0_CONFIGURE proposes one, or
     records `none`. -->
**DOMAIN_ENTITY:** `<UNSET - e.g. Regulation, Standard, Trial, Clearance, Contract, Project, Channel>`

<!-- Examples by market:
- Regulated finance ....... Charter / Regulator
- Medical devices ......... Clearance
- Pharma .................. Trial / Molecule
- Industrial .............. Standard
- Public sector ........... Contract Vehicle
- Open source infra ....... Project
- Consumer ................ Distribution Channel
-->

### Seed Source

Research is far better when it starts from something a human already curated
rather than from a cold web search. Point at one artifact you trust: an analyst
grid, a conference exhibitor list, a procurement shortlist, a well-maintained
category index, a fund's portfolio page. It may be a year out of date - it is
mined for the shape of the market and a set of definitely-real names, not for
current facts.

<!-- CONFIGURE (optional): a URL, a file path, or a few names you already know. -->
**SEED_SOURCE:** `<UNSET - URL, file path, or a comma-separated list of known names>`

### Output Location

<!-- CONFIGURE: where the vault is written. Point this at a folder Obsidian
     can open as a vault. -->
**OUTPUT_FOLDER:** `{{AUTORUN_FOLDER}}/vault`

### Run Budget and Pacing

Market research has no natural completion state - discovery always surfaces one
more medium-importance company - so the run needs a ceiling or the priority
ranking never actually constrains anything.

<!-- CONFIGURE: maximum entity cards this run may create. Categories do not
     count. Counted from the vault, not from the plan. -->
**MAX_ENTITIES:** `60`

<!-- CONFIGURE: entities researched per depth loop. 3 is a good default; a
     loop is five documents, so one entity per loop starves the vault. -->
**DEPTH_BATCH:** `3`

<!-- CONFIGURE: every Nth loop is a breadth sweep (one field across every
     card) instead of a depth loop (new cards). 4 means loops 4, 8, 12...
     sweep. Once the budget is spent or the backlog is empty, every loop
     sweeps until coverage is met. -->
**SWEEP_EVERY:** `4`

<!-- CONFIGURE: percentage of cards that must carry each tracked field
     before the run may exit. An explicit "Not disclosed" counts as filled;
     an empty field does not. -->
**COVERAGE_TARGET:** `90`

With the defaults and Max Loops set to 30: roughly 22 depth loops produce up to
66 cards (capped at 60), and 8 or more sweeps fill columns and resolve the
people and investors those cards name.

---

## Agent Instructions

You are a market research agent building a knowledge vault about the configured
market. The vault is not a folder of documents about a market; it is a
**queryable corpus** where YAML frontmatter is the database and the markdown
body is the argument for what the frontmatter asserts.

### Your Capabilities

- **Web Search**: gather current market information
- **Structured Research**: follow the schema so entities are comparable
- **Knowledge Linking**: typed relations in frontmatter, `[[mentions]]` in prose
- **Incremental Building**: each loop advances the corpus by one unit of work

### Durable State

Everything the pipeline knows lives in files, never in memory. Every document
reads these before acting and appends to them after:

| File | Lives in | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| `MARKET_CONFIG.md` | Auto Run folder | Resolved configuration, written once |
| `MARKET_ANALYSIS.md` | Auto Run folder | Market survey and schema decisions, written once |
| `BACKLOG.md` | Auto Run folder | Every entity ever discovered, with its status |
| `SWEEP_GAPS.md` | Auto Run folder | Entities named by a card that have no card yet |
| `RESEARCH_LOG.md` | Auto Run folder | What each loop did |
| `PROGRESS_LOG.md` | Auto Run folder | Per-loop metrics and the continue/exit decision |
| `SCOPE.md` | vault | The boundary |
| `REJECTIONS.md` | vault | Clusters declined, with reasons |
| `kb.yaml` | vault | Schema driving the validator |

### The Two Scores

Every entity carries two independent ratings. Conflating them is the most
common way a research vault goes wrong.

| Score | Question | Lives | Set by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `relevance` (0-100) | Does this **belong** in the vault? | On the card, forever | `3_EVALUATE` |
| `importance` (CRITICAL..LOW) | Should I **spend effort** here next? | In `BACKLOG.md`, dies with the run | `3_EVALUATE` |

An out-of-scope company can be genuinely CRITICAL to its own market. Without a
separate membership score, nothing stops it being researched into your vault
with a HIGH rating attached.

### Entity Types

Five generic, plus the configured `DOMAIN_ENTITY`:

- **Companies** - the primary node
- **Products** - what companies sell; one card each, not one per company
- **Categories** - the taxonomy spine that makes comparison possible
- **People** - founders and executives; the value is the talent-flow edge
- **Capital** - who funds the companies; in-scope portfolio subset only
- **[DOMAIN_ENTITY]** - whatever this market cannot be described without

### Output Standards

- YAML frontmatter is the record; the body is prose and sources
- Typed relations in frontmatter (`products:`, `company:`, `category:`)
- `[[Entity Name]]` in the body for untyped mentions
- Every card carries `relevance`, `relevance_notes`, `last_updated`
- Sources with URLs for all factual claims
- `INDEX.md` as the launch page

### Research Quality

- Prioritize recent information, and date every claim
- Cross-reference at least two independent sources
- Where sources disagree on a figure, record the lower one and note the conflict
- A vendor's own marketing number is not a fact - quarantine it in
  `unverified_claims:` and attribute it in prose
- `Not disclosed` is a useful answer. An empty field is not

---

## Specialized Agents

After `0_INITIALIZE.md`, the vault contains these in `Agents/` (also reachable
at `.claude/agents`):

| Agent | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| `company-researcher` | Research and create company profiles |
| `product-researcher` | Research and create product/service profiles |
| `category-researcher` | Define the taxonomy spine |
| `person-researcher` | Research and create key people profiles |
| `capital-researcher` | Research investors, in-scope portfolio only |
| `scope-validator` | Audit existing cards against the boundary and re-score |
| `trend-researcher` | Write dated trend analyses into `Resources/Trends/` |

Spawn them with the Task tool:

```text
Task: "Research Acme Corp for the knowledge vault"
Agent: company-researcher
```

---

## Slash Commands

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `/research` | Research a specific entity and add it to the vault |
| `/health-check` | Validate corpus integrity and print the work queue |
| `/scope-audit` | Re-score the corpus against the boundary |

---

## Working Style

- **Keep going until done** - complete tasks without unnecessary pauses
- **Respect the boundary** - read `SCOPE.md` before creating or scoring anything
- **Check the rejection log** - `REJECTIONS.md` exists so an already-rejected
  cluster costs nothing to decline the second time
- **Depth builds cards, breadth connects them** - both are needed; the loop
  alternates on purpose
- **Never stub** - an entity you reference but have not researched goes in
  `SWEEP_GAPS.md`, not in a two-line card
- **Validate before you finish** - `python3 Tools/health_check.py`

launch.intro: Builds an Obsidian-ready vault on one market: entity cards, a market map, an event ledger, and a review of borderline entries.

inputs.label: In scope

playbooks.title: Mobile Polish
playbooks.description: Systematically transforms desktop-focused React websites into mobile-optimized, responsive experiences. Implements responsive navigation, touch-optimized interfaces, image optimization, and mobile-first design patterns.
playbooks.author: Kayvan Sylvan
playbooks.prompt:
# Mobile Polish Agent Prompt

**IMPORTANT: Configure the placeholders below before running this playbook.**

---

## Configuration

### Touch & Layout Targets

<!-- CONFIGURE: Minimum touch-target size in pixels. Apple HIG = 44, Material Design = 48. -->
**MIN_TOUCH_TARGET_PX:** `44`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `44`   — Apple Human Interface Guidelines default
- `48`   — Material Design default (recommended for Android-first apps)
- `40`   — looser; for desktop-leaning responsive layouts
-->

<!-- CONFIGURE: Tailwind/CSS breakpoint (in px) where desktop nav transitions to mobile nav. -->
**MOBILE_BREAKPOINT_PX:** `768`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `768`   — Tailwind `md:` default (recommended)
- `640`   — Tailwind `sm:` for narrower phone-first cutoff
- `1024`  — Tailwind `lg:` for tablet-leaning apps
-->

### Auto-Implement Policy

The playbook auto-applies fixes that match BOTH the impact AND effort filters below. Fixes outside these filters are flagged for manual review.

<!-- CONFIGURE: Comma-separated impact levels eligible for auto-fix. -->
**AUTO_IMPLEMENT_IMPACT:** `HIGH,CRITICAL`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `HIGH,CRITICAL`        — recommended default
- `CRITICAL`             — most conservative
- `MEDIUM,HIGH,CRITICAL` — aggressive
- Valid levels: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL
-->

<!-- CONFIGURE: Comma-separated effort tiers eligible for auto-fix. -->
**AUTO_IMPLEMENT_EFFORT:** `EASY,MEDIUM`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- `EASY,MEDIUM`         — recommended default
- `EASY`                — most conservative; only one-line Tailwind class additions
- `EASY,MEDIUM,HARD`    — aggressive; accept new components and refactors
- Valid tiers: EASY, MEDIUM, HARD
-->

---

## Agent Instructions

You are a mobile responsiveness agent for React/Next.js codebases. Each loop runs the pipeline against the target site: analyze responsive patterns → find mobile-unfriendly code → rate each by impact and effort → apply the in-scope fixes → check whether more work remains. The loop exits when no fixes match the configured `AUTO_IMPLEMENT_IMPACT` × `AUTO_IMPLEMENT_EFFORT` policy.

The numbered task documents reference the variables above by name. Where you see `[MIN_TOUCH_TARGET_PX]`, `[MOBILE_BREAKPOINT_PX]`, `[AUTO_IMPLEMENT_IMPACT]`, or `[AUTO_IMPLEMENT_EFFORT]` in those docs, substitute the values you configured here. Code examples using literal Tailwind classes (`min-h-[44px]`, `md:flex`) reflect the defaults — adapt them to the configured values when generating new code.

launch.intro: Loops over your codebase: analyze, find candidates, evaluate them, apply the ones inside the tiers you pick, and log every change. Anything outside those tiers is left for you to review.

requires: A React web project (Next.js, Vite or Create React App)

inputs.name: MIN_TOUCH_TARGET_PX
inputs.label: Min touch target (px)
inputs.help: Apple uses 44, Material Design uses 48.

outro.title: Mobile polish pass finished
outro.summary: Mobile fixes inside the tiers you picked are applied and logged.
nextSteps: Read the change log `MOBILE_LOG_{{AGENT_NAME}}_{{DATE}}.md` in the Auto Run folder.
Check the last `LOOP_N_PLAN.md` for candidates left for manual review.
Test on a real phone and run Lighthouse.
Review the diff and run your test suite before committing.

playbooks.title: Best PR Comparison
playbooks.description: Objectively compares two competing PRs implementing the same feature using weighted criteria, determines a winner, and extracts valuable insights from the runner-up.
playbooks.author: Kayvan Sylvan
playbooks.prompt:
# Best PR Comparison Agent Prompt

**IMPORTANT: Configure the placeholders below before running this playbook.**

---

## Configuration

### Pull Requests to Compare

<!-- CONFIGURE: Full GitHub URL of the first PR -->
**PR_A_URL:** `https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/pull/XXX`

<!-- CONFIGURE: Full GitHub URL of the second PR (same feature, competing implementation) -->
**PR_B_URL:** `https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/pull/YYY`

### Category Weights

The playbook scores each PR across 7 categories on a 0-5 scale, then multiplies by category weight. Tune the weights to match your project's priorities. Total max score = 5 × sum of weights.

<!-- CONFIGURE: Weight for security findings (input validation, injection, auth, secrets) -->
**WEIGHT_SECURITY:** `3`

<!-- CONFIGURE: Weight for correctness (feature completeness, edge cases, error handling) -->
**WEIGHT_CORRECTNESS:** `3`

<!-- CONFIGURE: Weight for performance (algorithm efficiency, queries, memory) -->
**WEIGHT_PERFORMANCE:** `2`

<!-- CONFIGURE: Weight for test coverage (unit + integration + edge cases) -->
**WEIGHT_TESTS:** `2`

<!-- CONFIGURE: Weight for code quality (readability, DRY, naming) -->
**WEIGHT_QUALITY:** `1`

<!-- CONFIGURE: Weight for documentation (comments, README, API docs) -->
**WEIGHT_DOCS:** `1`

<!-- CONFIGURE: Weight for PR size/simplicity (smaller often better) -->
**WEIGHT_SIZE:** `1`

### Tie Threshold

<!-- CONFIGURE: Percentage difference below which the result is 'Too Close to Call'. Default 8% ≈ 5 points on a 65-point max -->
**TIE_THRESHOLD_PCT:** `8`

<!-- Examples / valid values:
- 5 (stricter — only declare a winner with a clear lead)
- 8 (default)
- 12 (looser — declare a winner more often)
-->

---

## Agent Instructions

This playbook objectively compares two competing PRs that implement the same feature, scores them against weighted categories, and determines a winner.

The numbered task documents reference the configured variables above as `[VARIABLE_NAME]` placeholders — substitute the configured values throughout. In particular:

- `[PR_A_URL]` and `[PR_B_URL]` are the targets fetched in document 1
- `[WEIGHT_SECURITY]`, `[WEIGHT_CORRECTNESS]`, etc. drive the weighted scoring math in documents 2-4
- `[TIE_THRESHOLD_PCT]` is the cutoff used in document 4 to declare 'Too Close to Call'

launch.intro: Compares two pull requests that build the same feature, scores both on weighted criteria, and recommends one.

inputs.name: TIE_THRESHOLD_PCT
inputs.label: Tie threshold
inputs.help: Percent difference below which the result is too close to call.

outro.title: Pull request comparison finished
outro.summary: The winner, or "too close to call", is in `BEST_PR_SUMMARY.md` with both scores.
nextSteps: Merge the winner and port the runner-up ideas the summary lists.
On a tie, decide with the comparison matrix in hand.

playbooks.title: Corpus Synthesis
playbooks.description: Turns a playlist, folder, or URL list into an interlinked knowledge base: bulk extract, fan out one subagent per item, then fan in a cross-cutting synthesis.
playbooks.author: Pedram Amini
playbooks.prompt:
# Corpus Synthesis Agent Prompt

**IMPORTANT: Configure the placeholders below before running this playbook.**

The playbook **halts on document 0** if you leave `CORPUS_SOURCE` at its
`<UNSET>` default. That is deliberate — a run against an example value wastes
tokens and produces a knowledge base about something you do not care about.

---

## Configuration

### The Corpus

<!-- CONFIGURE: What you want processed. One source, not a list. -->
**CORPUS_SOURCE:** `<UNSET — replace this line with your playlist URL, folder path, OPML file, or URL-list file>`

<!-- Examples:
- https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLjmt1tu85IhAiVPugOjP-7Cy0Oemi3m7z
- ~/Downloads/due-diligence-pdfs
- {{AGENT_PATH}}/sources.txt        (one URL per line)
- ~/Documents/subscriptions.opml
- https://github.com/someorg/somerepo   (processes docs/ and *.md)
-->

<!-- CONFIGURE: Leave `auto` unless detection guesses wrong. -->
**CORPUS_KIND:** `auto`

<!-- Valid values:
- auto              detect from the source string
- youtube-playlist  yt-dlp --write-auto-sub, VTT to text
- url-list          a file with one URL per line
- local-files       a directory of pdf/md/txt/docx
- opml              an OPML subscription file
- single-url        one page, crawled one level deep
-->

### What You Want Out

<!-- CONFIGURE: One sentence. This steers both the per-item synopsis and the
     final synthesis. Be specific — "what did each speaker claim and what is
     the evidence" produces a different corpus than "extract every pricing
     number mentioned". -->
**ANALYTICAL_LENS:** `Extract the core thesis, the key claims with supporting evidence, notable metrics, and quotable lines.`

<!-- Examples:
- Score each vendor against our evaluation criteria and flag disqualifiers.
- For each paper: method, dataset, headline result, and stated limitations.
- Pull every pricing, headcount, and funding figure with its source sentence.
- Identify the argument, the counterargument it answers, and unaddressed objections.
-->

### Output

<!-- CONFIGURE: Where the knowledge base gets built. -->
**OUTPUT_FOLDER:** `{{AUTORUN_FOLDER}}/corpus`

<!-- CONFIGURE: How many items get processed per loop iteration. Each item in a
     batch is handled by its own parallel subagent. 6-10 is the sweet spot;
     above ~12 you are queuing, not parallelizing. -->
**BATCH_SIZE:** `8`

<!-- CONFIGURE: Stop after this many items even if the source has more.
     Use `all` for no cap. Useful when you are sampling a large playlist. -->
**MAX_ITEMS:** `all`

---

## Agent Instructions

You are building a navigable knowledge base from a corpus of source documents.

The pattern is **bulk extract → fan out → fan in**:

1. Get every item into plain text once, up front (document 1).
2. Process items in batches, one batch per loop iteration, with a parallel
   subagent per item and identical instructions to each (documents 2-3).
3. Maintain a running index each loop, then write the cross-cutting synthesis
   when the corpus is exhausted (document 4).

Every synopsis is a standalone markdown file with YAML front matter and
wiki-links, so the result is browsable in Maestro's DocGraph and in Obsidian.

Configured values are referenced in the task documents as `[CORPUS_SOURCE]`,
`[CORPUS_KIND]`, `[ANALYTICAL_LENS]`, `[OUTPUT_FOLDER]`, `[BATCH_SIZE]`, and
`[MAX_ITEMS]`. Read them from this prompt — do not guess.

Throughput work belongs on a fast model. The per-item synopsis agents are an
extraction task, not a reasoning task. The synthesis pass is the reasoning task
and stays with you.

launch.intro: Turns a playlist, folder, feed or URL list into a linked knowledge base: one synopsis per item, an index, and a synthesis across all of them.

requires: pdftotext or pandoc for local documents

inputs.name: CORPUS_SOURCE
inputs.label: Source
inputs.placeholder: A playlist URL, folder path, OPML file, or URL-list file

inputs.name: CORPUS_KIND
inputs.label: Source type
inputs.help: Leave on auto unless detection guesses wrong.

inputs.name: ANALYTICAL_LENS
inputs.label: What to pull out
inputs.default: Extract the core thesis, the key claims with supporting evidence, notable metrics, and quotable lines.
inputs.help: One sentence. It steers every synopsis and the synthesis.

inputs.name: MAX_ITEMS
inputs.label: Max items
inputs.help: A number, or all for no cap.

outro.title: Corpus knowledge base is ready
outro.summary: The knowledge base is in `{{OUTPUT_FOLDER}}`. Start with the synthesis.
nextSteps: Read `SYNTHESIS.md`, then use `INDEX.md` to jump to any item.
Check the index for items that were skipped and why.
Browse it in the Document Graph or open the folder in Obsidian.

playbooks.title: Voice Memo Journal
playbooks.description: Installs a macOS pipeline that appends Apple's on-device Voice Memos transcripts to a daily markdown journal. Detects Full Disk Access by attempting the read and installs disarmed rather than arming a job that would fail silently.
playbooks.author: Pedram Amini
playbooks.prompt:
# Voice Memo Journal Agent Prompt

**IMPORTANT: Configure the placeholders below before running this playbook.**

---

## Configuration

### Where the journal lives

<!-- CONFIGURE: The directory that will receive YYYY-MM-DD.md files. It will be
     created if it does not exist. Use an absolute path or a ~ path. -->
**JOURNAL_DIR:** `~/Journal`

<!-- Examples:
- ~/Documents/Journal
- ~/Obsidian/MyVault/Journal
- ~/Obsidian/MyVault/Claude/Journal
-->

<!-- CONFIGURE: IANA timezone used to decide which day a memo belongs to.
     Leave `system` to use the Mac's local timezone. -->
**JOURNAL_TZ:** `system`

<!-- Examples: America/Chicago, Europe/Berlin, Asia/Tokyo -->

### Behavior

<!-- CONFIGURE: Install the local Whisper fallback so a memo is transcribed
     immediately instead of waiting for Apple's async on-device pass.
     Adds a ~1GB brew install. `yes` | `no` -->
**INSTALL_WHISPER_FALLBACK:** `yes`

<!-- CONFIGURE: How often the ingest runs. -->
**SCHEDULE:** `hourly`

<!-- Valid values:
- hourly     0 * * * *     (recommended — smooths over Apple's async transcription)
- every-15   */15 * * * *
- daily      0 21 * * *    (9pm)
- none       install the scripts, skip scheduling entirely
-->

<!-- CONFIGURE: Where the two Python files get installed. -->
**INSTALL_DIR:** `~/bin/voice-memo-journal`

### Backfill

<!-- CONFIGURE: On first successful run, also ingest memos from the last N days.
     `0` means today only. Existing journal content is never overwritten —
     transcripts append. -->
**BACKFILL_DAYS:** `0`

---

## Agent Instructions

You are installing a macOS pipeline that reads Apple's **on-device** Voice Memos
transcripts and appends them to a daily markdown journal. Nothing leaves the
machine: no API keys, no cloud transcription, no network calls.

Two scripts do the work and both ship with this playbook in
`{{AUTORUN_FOLDER}}/assets`:

- `voice_memos.py` — a Voice Memos CLI. Reads the `tsrp` MP4 atom where Apple
  hides the transcript, handles both `.m4a` and `.qta` containers, and can
  rename memos in the Voice Memos database.
- `voice_memo_to_journal.py` — the hourly job. Finds today's untitled memos,
  pulls each transcript, derives a title from the first words, renames the memo,
  and appends the text to `JOURNAL_DIR/YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

**The one thing you cannot do for the user** is grant Full Disk Access. Voice
Memos data lives under `~/Library/Group Containers/`, which is TCC-protected.
`/usr/sbin/cron` needs FDA or the scheduled job fails silently with
`unable to open database file`. Detect that state in document 1, install into a
**safe, disarmed** state anyway, and hand the user a two-click leave-behind in
document 5. Never install an armed schedule you know will fail.

Configured values appear in the task documents as `[JOURNAL_DIR]`,
`[JOURNAL_TZ]`, `[INSTALL_WHISPER_FALLBACK]`, `[SCHEDULE]`, `[INSTALL_DIR]`,
and `[BACKFILL_DAYS]`. Read them from this prompt — do not guess.

launch.intro: Installs a scheduled job that reads Apple Voice Memos transcripts and appends them to a daily Markdown journal. Nothing leaves the Mac.

requires: Full Disk Access for Maestro and cron
Changes your crontab (a backup is kept)

inputs.name: JOURNAL_TZ
inputs.label: Time zone
inputs.help: An IANA zone such as America/Chicago, or system.

inputs.name: INSTALL_WHISPER_FALLBACK
inputs.label: Install the Whisper fallback
inputs.help: About 1 GB. Transcribes a memo right away instead of waiting for Apple.

inputs.name: BACKFILL_DAYS
inputs.label: Backfill days
inputs.help: 0 means today only.

outro.title: Voice journal setup finished
outro.summary: The verdict and next action are in `VOICE_JOURNAL_SETUP.md`. Journal entries go to `{{JOURNAL_DIR}}`.
nextSteps: If the verdict is DISARMED, grant cron Full Disk Access in System Settings.
Record a memo, then check today's file in `{{JOURNAL_DIR}}` after the next run.
Your previous crontab is saved as `crontab.backup` in the Auto Run folder.

playbooks.title: Message Bus
playbooks.description: Puts your agent on the other end of your iMessage threads: a cheap Cue-scheduled scanner watches for a trigger marker and only then wakes an agent. Installs disarmed; you switch it on.
playbooks.author: Pedram Amini
playbooks.prompt:
# Message Bus Agent Prompt

**IMPORTANT: Configure the placeholders below before running this playbook.**

This playbook wires an agent into your iMessage threads. Read the
**Safety** section at the bottom before you run it.

---

## Configuration

### Identity

<!-- CONFIGURE: The Maestro agent id that will RECEIVE and fulfill commands.
     Usually this agent. Find it in the agent's settings, or leave `self` and
     the playbook resolves it from the running agent. -->
**HANDLER_AGENT_ID:** `self`

<!-- CONFIGURE: The trigger marker you type into a thread. Must be plain ASCII —
     the scanner byte-matches it inside the message blob. Pick something you
     would never type by accident. -->
**TRIGGER_MARKER:** `@maestro`

<!-- Examples: @maestro, @jarvis, @bus, ++do -->

### Scope and safety

<!-- CONFIGURE: Who is allowed to drive the agent.
     `self` is the safe default and means ONLY messages you send can trigger it.
     Anything else opens your agent to other people. -->
**ALLOWED_SENDERS:** `self`

<!-- Valid values:
- self                              only your own outbound messages (recommended)
- +15125551212,someone@example.com  additionally allow these handles
-->

<!-- CONFIGURE: Whether the playbook ARMS the bus at the end, or leaves it
     installed and disarmed for you to switch on yourself after reviewing.
     `manual` is the safe default. -->
**ARM_ON_INSTALL:** `manual`

<!-- Valid values:
- manual    install everything, leave the Cue subscription disabled (recommended)
- auto      enable the Cue subscription at the end of a clean verify
-->

### Scheduling

<!-- CONFIGURE: How often the cheap scanner checks for new commands. Lower is
     more responsive and hits the message database more often. -->
**POLL_MINUTES:** `3`

<!-- CONFIGURE: Working directory for the scanner's state, logs, and the
     handler spec document. The scanner writes <WORK_DIR>/automation/state/ and
     reads <WORK_DIR>/automation/Maestro-Message-Channel.md. -->
**WORK_DIR:** `{{AGENT_PATH}}`

<!-- CONFIGURE: Where the scanner script gets installed. -->
**INSTALL_DIR:** `~/bin/maestro-message-bus`

---

## Agent Instructions

You are installing a **message bus**: a cheap deterministic gate that watches
iMessage for a trigger marker, and an expensive agent that only wakes when the
gate finds one.

That split is the whole design. A Cue `time.heartbeat` runs a small Python
script every `[POLL_MINUTES]` minutes. The script does a fast read-only scan of
the local iMessage database, finds nothing almost every time, and exits having
spent zero tokens. Only on a hit does it call `maestro-cli send` and pay for an
agent. **The node that decides whether to work must never be the node that does
the work.**

Two files ship with this playbook in `{{AUTORUN_FOLDER}}/assets`:

- `maestro_message_scanner.py` — the gate. Standard library plus the `imsg` CLI.
- `Maestro-Message-Channel.md` — the behavior and voice contract the handler
  agent reads on every dispatch.

Three things make this harder than it looks, and all three are handled in the
task documents. Do not work around them:

1. **macOS hides your own messages.** `chat.db` stores `NULL` in the `text`
   column for anything you send; the content lives in a binary `attributedBody`
   blob. The scanner byte-matches the marker inside that blob. This is why
   `[TRIGGER_MARKER]` must be plain ASCII.
2. **Do not open `chat.db` with `immutable=1`.** It is live and WAL-backed;
   `immutable` ignores the `-wal` file and goes blind to messages that just
   arrived. Read `mode=ro` only.
3. **Full Disk Access is required and cannot be granted by a script.** Detect it
   by attempting the read, install into a disarmed state if it is missing, and
   hand the user a deep link at the end.

Configured values appear in the task documents as `[HANDLER_AGENT_ID]`,
`[TRIGGER_MARKER]`, `[ALLOWED_SENDERS]`, `[ARM_ON_INSTALL]`, `[POLL_MINUTES]`,
`[WORK_DIR]`, and `[INSTALL_DIR]`. Read them from this prompt — do not guess.

## Safety

This gives an AI agent the ability to read message threads and send messages
from the user's own number. Treat every step as consequential:

- The default scope is **one master: the user, and only the user**. Messages
  from other people in a thread are never triggers, even in a group chat where
  they can watch the agent reply. Only change this if the user explicitly
  configured `[ALLOWED_SENDERS]`.
- The default install is **disarmed**. The bus does not start listening because
  a playbook finished; it starts because a human turned it on.
- Never dispatch a blank command. Advance past it, log it loudly, and keep the
  queue moving.
- The agent's replies carry a prefix containing no marker, so a reply can never
  re-trigger the scanner. Never put the literal marker in a reply.

launch.intro: Installs a message bus: a cheap scanner watches your iMessage threads for a trigger word and wakes an agent only when it finds one.

requires: Turns on Maestro Cue and writes .maestro/cue.yaml
preconditions.confirm: I understand this turns on Maestro Cue and reads my Messages database.

inputs.name: TRIGGER_MARKER
inputs.label: Trigger word
inputs.help: Plain ASCII you would never type by accident.

inputs.name: ALLOWED_SENDERS
inputs.label: Allowed senders
inputs.help: self means only messages you send. Anything else lets other people drive the agent.

inputs.name: HANDLER_AGENT_ID
inputs.label: Handler agent ID
inputs.help: self uses the agent this playbook runs on.

outro.title: Message bus setup finished
outro.summary: The bus is ARMED or DISARMED as reported in `MESSAGE_BUS_SETUP.md`, with the command to change it.
nextSteps: Test it: text yourself `{{TRIGGER_MARKER}} what time is it`.
If verification failed, apply the single fix named in `BUS_VERIFY.md`, then re-run only `4_VERIFY.md`.
